name: Juvenile Dermatomyositis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Bohan and Peter Criteria (modified for juvenile dermatomyositis)

criteria.description: Elevated serum muscle enzymes (e.g., creatine kinase, aldolase)
Typical heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules
Muscle biopsy showing inflammation, necrosis, and perifascicular atrophy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of characteristic skin rash plus symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Muscle biopsy and EMG are supportive but not always required if clinical and laboratory findings are definitive.

pathognomonic.notes: Scaly erythematous papules over extensor surfaces of joints
Weakness predominantly affecting shoulder and hip girdle muscles
searchTerms: equal muscle weakness on both sides

common.notes: Calcium deposits in skin and soft tissues, more common with delayed treatment
Difficulty swallowing due to oropharyngeal muscle involvement

occasional.notes: Hyperkeratotic, fissured skin on lateral and palmar aspects of fingers
Vasospasm of fingers triggered by cold or stress

rare.notes: Pulmonary fibrosis or inflammation in severe cases

searchTerms: heart muscle inflammation and irregular heartbeat
heart rhythm problems with heart inflammation
heart involvement causing arrhythmias and myocarditis

rare.notes: Skin ulcerations due to calcium deposits

laboratory: Elevated serum creatine kinase (CK), aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and transaminases
Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) in some cases
imaging: MRI of muscles showing edema and inflammation
Chest X-ray or CT scan to evaluate for interstitial lung disease
genetic: No single causative gene; associations with HLA class II alleles (e.g., HLA-DRB1*03)
other: Muscle biopsy demonstrating perifascicular atrophy, inflammatory infiltrates, and muscle fiber necrosis
Electromyography showing myopathic motor unit potentials

distinguishingFeatures: Different muscle biopsy findings without perifascicular atrophy
Multisystem involvement with positive ANA and other lupus-specific antibodies
Different rash morphology (malar rash vs heliotrope)
Presence of infectious agents on biopsy or cultures
Rapid onset and systemic signs of infection

redFlags: Rapidly progressive muscle weakness with respiratory compromise
Development of calcinosis with skin ulcerations
references: Bohan A, Peter JB. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis (first of two parts). N Engl J Med. 1975;292(7):344-347.
Miller FW, Rider LG. Juvenile dermatomyositis: advances in pathogenesis and treatment. Curr Opin Rheumatol. 2005;17(6):675-680.
Rider LG, et al. Juvenile dermatomyositis: clinical features and pathogenesis. Nat Rev Rheumatol. 2018;14(5):279-292.
